[THOUGHT] The patient reports progressive, enlarging areas of skin lightening — a classic presentation of hypopigmentation or depigmentation. Key diagnostic considerations include vitiligo, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, pityriasis alba, tinea versicolor, and less commonly, systemic conditions (e.g., autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome). To narrow the differential, I need to assess morphology (e.g., well-demarcated vs. ill-defined borders), distribution (e.g., acral, periorificial, segmental), associated symptoms (pruritus, scaling, burning), and personal/family history of autoimmune disease or vitiligo. The next highest-yield question is about border characteristics and symmetry — vitiligo typically presents with sharply demarcated, often symmetrical, non-scaly patches.

[QUERY] Are the lighter patches well-defined (with clear, sharp edges) or more blurry/feathery at the borders?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure about the exact border characteristics—I haven’t specifically noticed whether the edges are sharp or blurry.

[THOUGHT] The patient is uncertain about border definition, so direct clinical observation would be more reliable than subjective description. Since physical exam is essential to assess border quality, symmetry, distribution, and presence of scaling or inflammation, the next best step is a targeted dermatologic examination — specifically inspecting the affected areas. Wood’s lamp examination is particularly valuable here: it enhances contrast in hypopigmented lesions and can help distinguish vitiligo (which typically shows bright, homogeneous fluorescence under Wood’s lamp) from other causes like tinea versicolor (which may show yellow-green fluorescence) or post-inflammatory changes (often dim or absent fluorescence).

This suggests either the test result is unavailable in the current context or the system requires a different approach. Since diagnostic progress is stalled without objective exam data, I must pivot to gathering high-yield clinical history that does not rely on testing. Key distinguishing features for vitiligo include Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at sites of trauma), associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes), and family history — all of which are strongly associated with non-segmental vitiligo. Asking about personal or family history of autoimmune disease is safe, efficient, and highly relevant.

[QUERY] Do you or any close family members have a history of autoimmune conditions — such as thyroid disease (e.g., Hashimoto’s or Graves’), type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata, or pernicious anemia?

[REFERENCE] 4. He also mentions that his father has a similar condition.  
[RESPONSE] My father has a similar skin condition — areas of lighter skin — but I don’t know if he has been diagnosed with any autoimmune conditions like thyroid disease, diabetes, alopecia areata, or pernicious anemia.

[THOUGHT] A family history of similar hypopigmented skin changes strongly supports a heritable, non-inflammatory pigmentary disorder — most consistent with vitiligo, which has well-documented familial clustering (up to 30% of patients report affected relatives). While autoimmune comorbidities would further support vitiligo, their absence doesn’t rule it out. Next, I need to assess distribution pattern — vitiligo commonly affects acral (fingers, toes), periorificial (lips, eyes, nostrils), and intertriginous areas; segmental vitiligo is rarer and unilateral. Also, presence of pruritus or scaling helps exclude inflammatory or infectious mimics (e.g., tinea versicolor often itches and scales; pityriasis alba is mildly scaly and facial). Since the patient hasn’t reported symptoms, asking about itch or scaling is efficient and discriminative.

[QUERY] Do any of the lighter patches itch, burn, or feel scaly or rough?

[REFERENCE] 7. No associated itchiness or discomfort.  
[RESPONSE] No, the lighter patches don’t itch, burn, or feel scaly or rough.

[THOUGHT] The absence of pruritus, scaling, or inflammation makes inflammatory (e.g., psoriasis, eczema), infectious (e.g., tinea versicolor), and post-inflammatory causes much less likely. The progressive, asymptomatic, enlarging hypopigmentation with family history strongly points to vitiligo — particularly non-segmental (generalized) vitiligo, the most common form. To further support this, I should assess distribution: vitiligo commonly involves sun-exposed and acral sites (fingers, wrists, face, lips, peri-orificial areas). Confirming involvement of these characteristic locations would increase diagnostic confidence without requiring additional tests. This is a high-yield, atomic question that can be answered quickly.

[QUERY] Are the lighter patches located on your face (especially around the mouth or eyes), hands, fingers, wrists, or feet?

[RESPONSE] I don’t recall the specific locations being mentioned — I just noticed several areas of lighter skin, but I wasn’t asked to note exactly where they are.

[THOUGHT] The patient is unable to specify anatomical locations — likely due to lack of focused self-assessment. Since distribution is critical for diagnosis and cannot be reliably obtained by history alone, the next best step is direct clinical evaluation. A targeted physical exam of common vitiligo sites (face, hands, peri-orificial areas, acral regions) will confirm presence/absence of lesions in characteristic locations and assess morphology (e.g., symmetry, border sharpness, depigmentation vs. hypopigmentation). This is more efficient than further questioning and avoids diagnostic delay.

[TEST] Physical examination of skin, with particular attention to face (lips, periorbital), hands (fingers, dorsum), wrists, and feet.

5. Multiple well-demarcated, hypopigmented macules and patches over the face, hands, and arms.  
6. No erythema or scale.  
7. Hair and nails are normal.  
8. Skin texture is normal within and around the lesions.  
9. No warmth or induration.

[THOUGHT] The physical exam findings are highly characteristic of vitiligo: well-demarcated, asymptomatic, non-scaly, non-inflammatory hypopigmented macules and patches distributed on face, hands, and arms — classic acral and periorificial predilection. Absence of erythema, scale, induration, or texture change rules out inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic mimics. Family history of similar skin changes further supports genetic/autoimmune etiology. While Wood’s lamp was not obtained, the constellation — progressive depigmentation, symmetry (implied by bilateral face/hands involvement), lack of symptoms, and family history — makes vitiligo overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis. No other condition fits this complete picture as precisely.

[DIAGNOSIS] Vitiligo
